title: What is a watermark (`withWatermark("event_time", "10 minutes")`) — it tells Spark how late data can arrive before being dropped and state for old windows is cleaned up — and why is it essential for bounding state in stateful streaming queries?
shortTitle: What is a watermark in Structured Streaming

s1_definition.profdef: A watermark is a moving threshold on event time that tells Spark how late an event may arrive before it is considered too old to process. You declare it with `withWatermark("eventTime", "10 minutes")`, and Spark continuously computes the watermark as the maximum event time seen so far minus the configured delay. Events with an event time older than the current watermark are dropped, and the state held for windows that have fully closed below the watermark is cleaned up. It is essential because in a stateful streaming query — windowed aggregations, stream-stream joins, deduplication — Spark would otherwise have to keep state for every open window forever, since any future event might belong to an old window; the watermark bounds that state by declaring a point past which late data is ignored.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India the central office must decide how long to keep an hour's tally open for late-arriving slips. The watermark is the rule: "we will wait up to ten minutes past the latest slip we have seen; anything older than that is too late and will not change closed tallies." Once the clock on the newest slip advances far enough, the office finalizes and files away the old hour's tally and stops holding paperwork for it. Without such a rule the office would have to keep every hour's tally open forever just in case a very old slip turns up, and the back room would overflow.
s1_definition.oneliner: A watermark is max-event-time-seen minus an allowed-lateness delay; events older than it are dropped and closed windows' state is cleaned up, which is what bounds state in stateful streaming.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A watermark is a moving threshold on event time that tells Spark how late an event may arrive before it is considered too old to process. You declare it with `withWatermark("eventTime", "10 minutes")`, and Spark continuously computes the watermark as the maximum event time seen so far minus the configured delay. Events with an event time older than the current watermark are dropped, and the state held for windows that have fully closed below the watermark is cleaned up. It is essential because in a stateful streaming query — windowed aggregations, stream-stream joins, deduplication — Spark would otherwise have to keep state for every open window forever, since any future event might belong to an old window; the watermark bounds that state by declaring a point past which late data is ignored.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India the central office must decide how long to keep an hour's tally open for late-arriving slips. The watermark is the rule: "we will wait up to ten minutes past the latest slip we have seen; anything older than that is too late and will not change closed tallies." Once the clock on the newest slip advances far enough, the office finalizes and files away the old hour's tally and stops holding paperwork for it. Without such a rule the office would have to keep every hour's tally open forever just in case a very old slip turns up, and the back room would overflow.

**One line to remember:** A watermark is max-event-time-seen minus an allowed-lateness delay; events older than it are dropped and closed windows' state is cleaned up, which is what bounds state in stateful streaming.

sections.s2_technical:
The watermark is computed from the data, not the clock. Spark tracks the maximum event-time value it has observed across the stream, and the current watermark equals that maximum minus the delay you configured. So with a ten-minute delay, if the latest event seen has event time 11:20, the watermark is 11:10, meaning Spark now assumes it will not see events older than 11:10. As newer events push the maximum up, the watermark advances monotonically; it never moves backward.

Two things happen relative to the watermark. First, any incoming event whose event time is below the current watermark is treated as too late and dropped from aggregation, because the window it belongs to is assumed finalized. Second, the state Spark holds for windows that end before the watermark is cleaned up, because no further events can update them. This second effect is the one that bounds memory in a long-running stateful query.

You declare it with `stream.withWatermark("eventTime", "10 minutes")` before the aggregation, and it only has meaning when combined with event-time operations like a windowed groupBy, a stream-stream join, or dropDuplicates over an event-time column. The delay string is the allowed lateness. The watermark column must be the same event-time column used in the window, and it must be a timestamp type.

The watermark also interacts with output mode. In Append mode with aggregation, a window's result is emitted only once the watermark passes the end of the window, because Append requires that an emitted row is final; the watermark is exactly what tells Spark the window is final. In Update mode, intermediate results can be emitted before finalization, but the watermark still governs when state is dropped and when truly late events are ignored. This is why Append aggregation without a watermark is rejected at query start.

A senior-level nuance is the tuning trade-off and the consequence of getting it wrong. A larger delay captures more late events and improves completeness but keeps state longer and delays finalization, raising memory and latency. A smaller delay finalizes quickly and uses less memory but silently drops more late events, which in a bank can mean undercounting. You size the delay to the real lateness distribution of the feed — often around the high-percentile observed delay — and you monitor dropped-late-event metrics so you can tell whether the watermark is too tight. The watermark is therefore a deliberate correctness-versus-resource control, not a default you set and forget.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a per-minute windowed count of transactions over an infinite stream. Without a watermark, Spark keeps the state for every minute forever, and memory grows without bound until the job dies. A watermark lets Spark finalize and drop old minutes' state.

Problem 2 — Some transactions arrive genuinely late. The bank is willing to wait ten minutes for stragglers but not longer, because downstream reports must close. The watermark encodes that ten-minute tolerance precisely.

Problem 3 — Operations need to know how many events were dropped for being too late, to confirm the watermark is not silently discarding real data. The job should surface a dropped-late count.

The demo simulates a moving watermark as events arrive with varying event times, applies the drop rule, counts per window, cleans up windows that fall below the watermark, and reports how many events were dropped as too late.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: batch 1 has events at minutes 60, 61, 62. Batch 2 has a minute-75 event and a minute-50 straggler. The watermark delay is ten minutes.

Step 1: Batch 1 is processed. The maximum event minute is 62, so the watermark is 52. All three events are at or above 52, so none are dropped, and open windows are minute 60 with one, minute 61 with one, minute 62 with one.

Step 2: State cleanup runs: no window is below 52, so nothing is cleaned. The aggregator logs watermark 52 and the three open windows.

Step 3: Batch 2 is processed. The minute-75 event pushes the maximum to 75, so the watermark advances to 65. The minute-50 straggler is below 65, so it is dropped as too late and the dropped-late counter increments.

Step 4: State cleanup removes every open window below 65, so minutes 60, 61 and 62 are finalized and dropped, leaving only minute 75 with one. This is how the watermark bounds state — old windows are released once the watermark passes them.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 05:09:00 INFO    Watermark=52 openWindows={60=1, 61=1, 62=1}
2026-10-30 05:09:00 WARNING Dropped late event in minute 50 (watermark 65)
2026-10-30 05:09:00 INFO    Watermark=65 openWindows={75=1}
2026-10-30 05:09:00 INFO    Final open windows: {75=1}
2026-10-30 05:09:00 INFO    Total dropped-late events: 1
2026-10-30 05:09:00 INFO    Watermark demo complete.
```

```
  track max event minute ── minus delay(10) ──→ watermark (monotonic ↑)
    │
    ├─ eventMinute < watermark ? ──yes──→ DROP (too late), droppedLate++
    │
    └─ else ──→ merge into windowState[minute]++

  open windows emitted / finalized
    batch1: wm=52 → {60,61,62 open}
    batch2: wm=65 → {60,61,62 finalized+dropped}, {75 open}, minute50 dropped
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A watermark is a moving threshold on event time that tells Spark how late an event may arrive before it is treated as too old. You declare it with withWatermark on the event-time column and an allowed-lateness delay, and Spark computes the current watermark as the maximum event time it has seen minus that delay. The watermark only advances, never moves backward. Two things happen against it: any event older than the current watermark is dropped from the aggregation, and the state for any window that ends before the watermark is cleaned up because no further events can change it.

That second effect is why the watermark is essential for stateful streaming. In a windowed aggregation, a stream-stream join, or a deduplication, Spark must hold state, and without a watermark it would have to keep every window's state forever, because in principle any future event could belong to an old window. The watermark declares a point past which late data is ignored, so Spark can finalize and release old state and keep memory bounded over a long-running job. It also pairs with output mode: in Append mode a windowed result is emitted only once the watermark passes the window's end, which is why Append aggregation without a watermark is rejected at query start.

At the National Bank of India I used a ten-minute watermark on a per-minute windowed transaction count. It let the job wait ten minutes for stragglers, then finalized and dropped each minute's state so memory stayed flat over days of running, and it dropped events that were genuinely too late. I sized the delay to roughly the high-percentile observed lateness of the feed and monitored the dropped-late metric so I could tell if the watermark was too tight and silently discarding real data. In interviews I summarize it as: the watermark is max-event-time-seen minus allowed lateness, it drops too-late events and evicts closed-window state, and it is the one mechanism that keeps stateful streaming state from growing without bound.
